20.0.0.en: 1- “The Lord hear thee in the day of trouble; the name of the God of Jacob defend thee;”

20.0.1.en: 1- Affliction is a hard thing and troubles a person, but in it he experiences the work of God and rejoices in fellowship with Him, so the distress becomes a cause of blessing and spiritual growth for the person, and even an experience of the Kingdom while he is on earth.

20.0.2.en: 2- For affliction, or distress, to be lifted, a person must pray and strive, like Jacob the father of the fathers, who wrestled with God and received the blessing. God answers him who cries to Him, and not the slothful.

20.0.3.en: 3- David prays to God during his distress, but he also needs the prayers of the people for him, so they say to him, “The Lord hear thee.”

20.0.4.en: 4- The God who will give David victory, as He gave Jacob victory of old when he wrestled with Him, is a tangible and real God, who has a name; He is not imagination but a lived reality, experienced by the fathers throughout the generations, seen by Jacob, and felt by David when he killed Goliath (1 Sam 17:45).

20.0.5.en: 5- This verse is David's confession of his weakness and his need of God, who is able to answer him and give him victory, as Jacob confessed his weakness before the strength of Esau and clung to God and He blessed him, and as he pleaded with God and He delivered him from the hand of his uncle Laban (Gen 31:24).

20.0.6.en: 6- This verse shows the people's love for their king in their prayers for him, and this rejoices God's heart, that the leader loves his people and the people their leader, so He hastens to answer.

20.0.7.en: 7- The day of trouble and affliction is the day of the Cross, while the victory that was accomplished on the Cross appeared in the Resurrection and the Ascension. And as we feel affliction in this life, we feel victory when God delivers us from sin, and then the victory is completed in reaching eternity.

20.0.8.en: 8- David's prayer represents individual prayer, and the people's prayer represents communal prayer, and when the two are joined God answers and gives victory, for God rejoices in both kinds of prayer.

20.1.0.en: 2- “Send thee help from the sanctuary, and strengthen thee out of Zion;”

20.1.1.en: 1- God feels for you and sends you help at the right time, and if He delays it is so that your striving and your clinging to Him may increase, and you may afterward receive greater help and experience His love more fully.

20.1.2.en: 2- God's sanctuary is heaven, where He dwells, and heavenly help is very strong help, which covers you and protects you, and no one can resist it.

20.1.3.en: 3- God's sanctuary is the ark of the covenant, which symbolizes the Church, where the altar and the sacrament of the Eucharist are, and this is the greatest power that supports you against the wars of the devil.

20.1.4.en: 4- Zion is also the Church, where the believers gather and lift up communal prayers, which support every striver among the members of the Church in his life and striving.

20.1.5.en: 5- Zion is the human soul, for God strengthens man within him, so that he feels the power of God supporting him and is at peace even in the midst of distress.

20.2.0.en: 3- “Remember all thy offerings, and accept (make fat) thy burnt sacrifice; Selah.”

20.2.1.en: 1- God in love does not forget the former offerings that David offered; He forgets no love offered to Him, and stretches out to him His hand with blessing and help at the time of man's need.

20.2.2.en: 2- God makes your burnt offerings fat, that is, He sees them as fat, even if they are small, but in His eyes they are great, as He saw the greatness of the gift of the widow with her two mites (Lk 21:3), and likewise the two fishes and five loaves (Jn 6:9), and also the cup of cold water, whose reward is not lost before God (Mt 10:42).

20.2.3.en: 3- Sacrifices are what a person offers and others share with him, eating of them, so they symbolize a person's love for those around him; but the burnt offering is burned entirely to please God, so it symbolizes a person's love for God. God rejoices in our love for Him and our love for others.

20.2.4.en: 4- When a person sees Christ crucified, he feels that he wants to offer his life as a sacrifice of love to God, indeed a burnt offering for Him, that is, to give his life in prayer, worship and service.

20.2.5.en: 5- The word Selah is a musical pause, in which we lift our hearts to God that He may accept our worship, our striving and our small service, which He sees as great by His love and His fatherhood toward us.

20.3.0.en: 4- “Grant thee according to thine own heart, and fulfil all thy counsel.”

20.3.1.en: 1- The giver of every good thing in a person's life is God; so he must lift up his heart with thanksgiving to God at all times. It is good for a person to ask of God, but it is better not to forget to thank God after he receives the gift, so that he is not proud, or ascribes it to himself, or to others, or to circumstances.

20.3.2.en: 2- God is ready to give you all that you desire, that is, according to your heart, if your heart desires and accepts the will of God; but if your will is contrary to God, He will not give it to you, because His will is the salvation of your soul, so if your will is contrary, that is, you seek the world that keeps you from God, He will not answer you.

20.3.3.en: 3- If you have counsels and have begun to carry them out, do not worry about completing them, because God who loves you will complete for you what you began, as long as you hold fast to His commandments.

20.3.4.en: Be at peace, for God is your shepherd, and your heavenly Father is with you; He will not leave you, but gives you what you ask and what you desire. Only be submissive to Him, hold fast to His word, and be steadfast in His Church, and even if afflictions pass over you, you will come out of them with more strength.

20.4.0.en: 5- “We will rejoice in thy salvation, and in the name of our God we will set up our banners: the Lord fulfil all thy petitions.”

20.4.1.en: 1- When God saves a person from distress he must sing and thank God, that is, express his joy in words of praise and thanksgiving to God.

20.4.2.en: 2- Deliverance from distress is the first thing that makes a person glad, but greater than it is deliverance from sin and the enjoyment of eternal salvation, that is, he thanks God that He has prepared the Kingdom for him, and he receives it through the Church and its sacraments and means of grace.

20.4.3.en: 3- There was an ancient Eastern custom that if a man killed another and then fled and sheltered in a city, or with some great person, and then reconciliation became possible between him and the family of the one killed, he would raise a banner in which he proclaimed his deliverance and reconciliation, and the pardon of those who had the right to take vengeance on him. So we raise a banner in the name of our God, who saved us from Satan, who wants to kill us and holds our sins against us. Christ lifted from us the sentence of death and gave us acquittal from sin; therefore we glorify Christ our God and lift up His Cross, which is our banner, our salvation and our victory.

20.4.4.en: 4- If we began by thanking and glorifying God who saved us from distress, we must after this love Him and cling to Him, because we discover the extent of His love and care for us, so that we live in praising Him forever; so you love God the Giver more than the gift, and the One who gave us victory more than the victory and success.

20.4.5.en: 5- In the spirit of prophecy David sees not only God who gives him victory over his enemies, but Christ the Redeemer, who comes in the fullness of time and saves mankind from the chains of sin and opens to them the closed gates of Paradise.

20.4.6.en: 6- When a person feels at peace through praising God his Savior, he is encouraged and asks of God, who answers him and completes His gifts to him in all that he asks according to His divine will.

20.5.0.en: 6- “Now know I that the Lord saveth his anointed; he will hear him from his holy heaven with the saving strength of his right hand.”

20.5.1.en: 1- David felt that God is his Savior; his anointed means David the king, anointed as king by the pouring of oil on his head by the hand of Samuel the prophet. During his prayer he felt peace and rest that God is his Savior and will always save him, so it is a prayer full of faith and hope.

20.5.2.en: 2- His anointed means also our Lord Jesus Christ, who was anointed by the Holy Spirit in the river Jordan at His baptism, and the Lord saved Him from death by His Resurrection, for He raised Himself by the power of His divinity.

20.5.3.en: 3- Likewise the word “his anointed” applies to every believer in the New Testament, who has been anointed by the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Holy Myron; God saves him from all his troubles, and he feels rest and peace when he prays, so he is not disturbed by any distress that may come upon him in the future.

20.5.4.en: 4- God rejoices in the prayers of His children and answers them from His holy heaven, that is, the heaven in which God's throne is, and this is a declaration of God's power and loftiness and His ability to answer our prayers. His holy heaven is also the womb of the Virgin, for she is the second heaven, which was sanctified by the divine conception, and by His Incarnation He saved us from our sins and redeemed us. Likewise His holy heaven is His temple, which is the holiest place in the world, or heaven on earth, for He rejoices in the prayers of His children in the Church and answers them.

20.5.5.en: 5- God's power to answer mightily is stronger than we imagine, and He expresses this power by His right hand, which is able to save us from our troubles and give us depths we cannot imagine in His love and fellowship.

20.5.6.en: 6- And at the right hand of the Father the Son sat, so here he prophesies about Christ the Mighty and Powerful, who offers salvation to mankind in the fullness of time.

20.6.0.en: 7- “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the Lord our God.”

20.6.1.en: 1- Here David speaks of the enemies of the people of God, whether the Egyptians under the leadership of Pharaoh (Ex 14:28), or the Syrians who fought David (2 Sam 8:6), or, in the spirit of prophecy, the Assyrians under the leadership of Sennacherib (Isa 37:36). All these enemies relied on strength in war, represented by horses and chariots. But the people of God relied on remembering His holy name, which overcomes the enemies however great their strength.

20.6.2.en: 2- The chariots and horses symbolize the body, and this is what Satan fights; but the spirit lives and is strengthened by the name of the Lord, so it can overcome the lusts of the body, control them, subdue the body and lead it in the way of God.

20.6.3.en: 3- This verse applies, in the spirit of prophecy, to the Apostles and servants of the New Testament, who by the name of the Lord overcame the power of the demons and spread Christianity among the pagans. It applies also to the monks of the desert, who cleansed it of demons by the name of the Lord and triumphed over the various lusts.

20.7.0.en: 8- “They are brought down and fallen: but we are risen, and stand upright.”

20.7.1.en: 1- When God entered the war with His people the enemies fell, and David the prophet says of them “they are brought down,” that is, they knelt and fell and were thrown on the ground. This is what happened with the Egyptians at the bottom of the Red Sea, when the water covered them and they drowned and died, because they relied on their strength and did not believe in God.

20.7.2.en: 2- The people of God relied on the power of God, so they rose and stood upright and came out of the Red Sea with a great victory, and so in all the wars the enemies would fall and they would be exalted above them.

20.7.3.en: 3- In the spiritual war the demons fall, but God's children by His power rise and come out of every distress, and if they fall because of their weakness God raises them, and they stand upright and thank Him.

20.7.4.en: 4- If the beginning of the Psalm in (v. 1) mentions the trouble and distress through which Christ passed, which is His Cross, in this verse he declares that by the power of Christ the children of God bear the Cross, and they rise and stand upright by His Resurrection.

20.7.5.en: Trust, for you are a child of God and your natural position is to be standing upright; if you fall into sin, this is a position foreign to you, so repent and return to God, and you will rise and return to your natural position. And if the marks of distress appear in your life do not be troubled, because God who rose from the dead dwells in you, and comforts you, and strengthens you, and keeps your peace until the distress ends.

20.8.0.en: 9- “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call.”

20.8.1.en: 1- He concludes the Psalm with a call upon God to save whom? The king, the rulers, the teachers and all the people, for God is able to deliver all His people and save them continually from all enemies.

20.8.2.en: 2- David addresses God and calls Him King, and this is the first time we find a man addressing God with this title, and after him Isaiah the prophet, who said that God is the King (Isa 6:5). So he asks God, who has authority, to answer him on the day he calls upon Him and seeks Him.

20.8.3.en: 3- Whoever has God reigning over his heart, and controls his senses and thoughts, can respond to the requests and needs of others when they ask him for help, because he is rid of selfishness by God's reigning over his heart, which gives him the spirit of giving and self-sacrifice.

20.8.4.en: 4- God is ready to answer if we ask Him, but if we are slothful, or our faith is weak and we do not ask Him, we will receive nothing.

20.8.5.en: 5- It is our duty to ask on behalf of our kings and rulers, and all our spiritual and worldly leaders, that the Lord may give them grace and wisdom, so that we may live in peace. And because the wars of the demons are stronger against rulers, it is our duty to ask for them.

20.8.6.en: Ask of God all that you need, for He is your Father who loves you and hastens to meet your requests. And do not forget to ask on behalf of others and everyone who has responsibility, that God may support him in it.

20.8.8.en: To the chief musician. A psalm of David. “The king shall joy in thy strength, O Lord” ... (v. 1) Introduction:

20.8.9.en: 1- When was it written? After David's victory over the children of Ammon in the city of Rabbah (2 Sam 12:26-31).

20.8.10.en: 2- When is it said? At the coronation of kings in the kingdom of Judah; the priest would repeat the words of this Psalm except verses 8 and 13, with which the people respond to the priest; all of this is said to the king.

20.8.11.en: 3- This Psalm is one of the Messianic Psalms; it speaks of Christ after His victory over Satan, His Resurrection from the dead and His Ascension.

20.8.12.en: 4- This Psalm completes the previous Psalm: if the twentieth Psalm speaks of David's distress before the battle, this Psalm speaks of his victory after the battle. And if the twentieth Psalm speaks of the distress of the Cross, this Psalm speaks of the Resurrection. And if the twentieth Psalm speaks of the distress in the life of any spiritual person, this Psalm speaks of his thanksgiving to God after his victory in the spiritual war.

20.8.13.en: 5- This Psalm speaks of the gifts granted to the spiritual striver, or to the king who trusts in God.

20.8.14.en: 6- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
